big: A client wants to move ₹10 lakh from one fund to another with a better record. She thinks it is a simple switch. It is a sale and a purchase. It can bring tax and an exit load, which may cost more than the new fund's edge.

lines: It is only a switch inside the same fund house. Why would there be tax?
In law, a switch is a redemption followed by a fresh purchase. Tax may apply on the gain, and an exit load may apply if you leave early. Compare that cost with what the new fund may add.

note: Units are sold first-in, first-out. The oldest units are treated as sold first. Rates and limits are as per current rules and change with Budgets. Confirm each year.

title: FIFO and switching
stops: A switch between schemes is not a sale
Regular to direct is a transfer too
Exit load never applies on a switch
caps: The oldest units are treated as sold first.
A switch is a redemption plus a fresh purchase.
Tax and load may apply here as well.
Load applies to the amount switched, within its period.

q: A client sells part of a holding bought in three lots over two years. Which units are treated as sold first?
why: The newest units would be last-in, first-out, which is not used.
Price does not decide the order of sale. The details here point elsewhere.
First-in, first-out treats the oldest units as sold first.
Cost does not decide the order of sale. It does not fit the facts given.

q: Meena switches from one scheme to another within the same fund house. How is it treated?
opts: A redemption plus a fresh purchase
A name change of the same units
A bonus issue of extra new units
why: A switch is treated as selling one scheme and buying another.
Tax may apply, so it is not a tax-neutral move.
It involves a real sale and purchase, not a rename.
A bonus issue gives extra units, which is unrelated.

q: A client wants to move from a regular plan to a direct plan of the same scheme. What should the adviser say?
opts: It has no cost, as it is one fund
It resets the NAV to zero at once
It is allowed only on bank holidays
A transfer, so tax and load may apply
why: It may carry tax and load, so it is not without cost.
The NAV is not reset to zero by a switch. It does not fit the facts given.
Holidays have no link to this. It does not answer what was asked.
Plan switches are treated as transfers, so costs may arise.

q: Before recommending a switch, what should the adviser compare?
opts: The colour of the logo and the brochure
Tax and load against the new fund's benefit
The number of ads that the new fund house ran
The fund manager's age and hometown
why: A logo's colour has nothing to do with the decision.
The cost of switching must be weighed against what the new fund adds.
Advertising volume does not show benefit. The details here point elsewhere.
A manager's age is not the test. That does not match this case.

pts: A switch, even to a direct plan, is a sale plus a fresh purchase.
Compare tax and exit load with the benefit before switching.
